ai-at-work.title: We don’t need AI regulation — leave safety to us, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says
ai-at-work.excerpt: AI isn't some new form of "alien mind," according to Jensen Huang. It's just hardware and software, so safety can be engineered by each AI product maker.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Jensen Huang says companies like Nvidia don't need government regulation on AI because they can self-regulate safety through engineering. This matters to digital workplace pros because AI tools are already embedded in your collaboration platforms, content management systems, and employee communications, so whether safety standards exist at the industry or regulatory level directly impacts what your organization can actually trust and deploy. I've been doing this for 30 years, and I've never seen "leave it to the vendors to police themselves" work out well, especially when quarterly earnings are on the line.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google have been in talks on AI safety for weeks
ai-at-work.excerpt: OpenAI confirms weeks of AI safety talks with Anthropic and Google DeepMind, as Trump's team dismisses safety concerns and pushes to keep pace with China.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The three biggest AI labs have been quietly coordinating on safety standards while the incoming administration dismisses those very concerns as obstacles to competition. This matters because digital workplace professionals will be deploying these tools into their organizations, and whoever sets the safety baseline now shapes what risks land on your desk later. It's like watching three pilots agree on how to maintain the plane while someone in the cockpit yells to just fly faster and ignore the warning lights.

ai-at-work.title: Cohesity’s new Agent Resilience lets companies roll back AI agents that go wrong
ai-at-work.excerpt: Data security company Cohesity Inc. today introduced Cohesity Agent Resilience at its Catalyst conference. The new Cohesity Data Cloud capability backs up the memory and configuration of enterprise ar
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Cohesity just released a backup and rollback feature for AI agents, letting companies revert them to a known good state when they inevitably go haywire. This matters because we're about to deploy a lot of AI agents into our digital workplaces, and having a panic button when they start making weird decisions feels pretty essential. Finally, someone's building the undo button we all knew we'd need the moment we started letting machines make autonomous choices in production.

ai-at-work.title: OpenAI, Anthropic and Google secretly joined forces to collaborate on AI safety
ai-at-work.excerpt: OpenAI Group PBC’s global head of policy Chris Lehane said today that his company has been working closely with rivals Anthropic PBC and Google LLC’s DeepMind research lab to try to devise a framework
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Three major AI companies quietly started working together on safety frameworks instead of competing on this critical issue. This matters because whatever safety standards these giants agree on will likely become the de facto baseline for AI tools flooding into enterprise environments, whether your IT team likes it or not. Secretly collaborating on safety is refreshingly honest, though calling it "secret" while announcing it at a press conference is like sneaking into a party and immediately telling everyone.

tools-tech.title: The latest Windows 11 update may mess with your device’s audio – here’s the workaround
tools-tech.excerpt: The September Patch Tuesday update is causing audio problems with certain USB devices, but you may be able to resolve it yourself.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's September Patch Tuesday update is breaking audio on some USB devices, and users are left hunting for workarounds instead of getting a proper fix. For digital workplace pros, this matters because audio issues directly tank video calls, training sessions, and conference presentations, which suddenly become everyone's problem when they happen at scale across your organization. After three decades watching Microsoft patch cycles, I can tell you this is peak tech comedy: they release an update to fix security holes, punch new ones in audio, then ask you to play detective in your spare time.

tools-tech.title: Tech layoffs: A 2026 timeline
tools-tech.excerpt: Among a range of factors leading to a wave of tech sector layoffs in 2026 is the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and automation. Companies are reconfiguring their workforces to leverage AI for i
tools-tech.dwp_take: Tech companies are laying off workers in 2026 despite strong profits, driven mostly by AI adoption and automation replacing human roles. Digital workplace leaders need to understand this isn't temporary belt-tightening but structural change, which means your tech stack, employee experience strategy, and internal communications approach all need rethinking. Here's the thing though: companies cutting staff while posting record earnings aren't being forced into it by market conditions, they're choosing it, and that tells you everything you need to know about where priorities actually sit.

tools-tech.title: Tech CEOs used to fear their boards. No more
tools-tech.excerpt: The colorful CEO of Automattic, which controls WordPress, was forced out last Thursday by his board of directors, which put him on a leave of absence. He used his system access to remove the accounts
tools-tech.dwp_take: Matt Mullenweg got booted from Automattic's CEO role by his board, used admin access to remove rival executives' accounts, and then got reinstated within days anyway. This matters because it shows boards have completely lost the ability to enforce accountability at the top, which sets a terrible precedent for governance and employee trust across tech companies. When a CEO can literally sabotage his own company's systems and face zero real consequences, you know the inmates are running the asylum.

tools-tech.title: General Robotics takes a new approach to building a robotic brain
tools-tech.excerpt: When it comes to building robotic brains, many companies in the industry focus on putting intelligence directly into their robots. General Robotics is taking an alternate approach. The Redmond, WA com
tools-tech.dwp_take: General Robotics is moving robotic intelligence from individual machines into the cloud with their GRID system, letting remote robots tap into centralized AI brains rather than carrying their own processing power. This matters to us because it's the same architectural shift we're seeing in workplace tech generally, where local processing gives way to cloud-hosted intelligence that scales faster and updates everywhere simultaneously. The irony is thick though: we spent decades moving compute closer to users for speed, and now we're sending it back to the cloud because that's where the actual brains live.

digital-culture.title: A manager rejected a top candidate over one tool. It backfired immediately
digital-culture.excerpt: Hiring the right person is hard. Learning to be an end user on most commercially available software is not hard. Bryan Creely, a former recruiter and currently cofounder and CEO of Soor, shared a time
digital-culture.dwp_take: A manager rejected a top candidate because they lacked experience with a specific software tool, even though the candidate was otherwise perfectly qualified for the role. This matters to digital workplace folks because it highlights how poorly we've calibrated our hiring filters: we're optimizing for tool proficiency instead of capability and adaptability, which is backwards. Here's the truth: if you're passing on talented people because they haven't used your particular flavor of project management software, you deserve the mediocre team you're about to build.

digital-culture.title: Sabbaticals are a powerful retention tool. Here’s the research to prove it
digital-culture.excerpt: Formal sabbatical policies are increasingly attractive for employees, but are often misunderstood by companies considering them. Giving employees more than a vacation—months, not days or weeks—provide
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study shows that formal sabbatical programs (we're talking months, not weeks) actually reduce burnout and improve retention better than traditional vacation policies. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally realizing that burnt-out employees don't engage with your shiny new collaboration tools no matter how good they are. Honestly, it's wild that we needed research to prove that letting people actually rest makes them want to stick around, but here we are.

digital-culture.title: Workforce data, smarter AI integration among greatest workplace priorities in the new year
digital-culture.excerpt: The importance of workforce data is just one of the prognostications people managers are making looking to the year ahead.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are finally admitting that they need better workforce data and smarter ways to integrate AI into their operations to stay competitive in 2025. This matters because digital workplace pros have been drowning in disconnected systems and half-baked AI implementations for years, and now leadership is actually willing to fund solutions that might actually work. Of course, the real question is whether these same people managers will still be using Excel spreadsheets and asking HR to manually count heads by next November.

digital-culture.title: Why the Postpandemic Tech Bust Sent Billionaires to Trump
digital-culture.excerpt: Following mass layoffs in 2022 and 2023, many tech workers turned against their employers. When liberal politicians also rallied against Silicon Valley, their backers turned to Donald Trump.
digital-culture.dwp_take: A bunch of tech billionaires who got burned by their own hiring and firing disasters figured out that Democratic politicians weren't going to be their cheerleaders anymore, so they pivoted hard toward Trump. This matters because it signals how quickly tech money and influence can realign when business conditions shift and political winds change, which affects everything from regulation to talent policy. Here's the thing: these billionaires didn't suddenly become principled conservatives. They just realized their previous political bets weren't paying dividends, so they're shopping around like everyone else.
